85.title: The hare in the moon
85.hook: a hare with nothing to give offers himself to a hungry guest; his image is set on the moon (Jataka 316)
85.howItsDone: Jataka tales like the hare's are told to children, painted on temple walls and performed as plays across Buddhist Asia, and Buddhists hear in them the perfections, such as generosity, that the Buddha is said to have practiced over many lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, parinibbana, and the last words: all things put together come apart, so keep going. Your line was strive on with care. Day eighty-five, and a new week: the Jataka, as shorts.

Tonight, if the sky is clear, look up at the moon. In the West people often see a face. In much of Asia, many people see a rabbit. We've just walked with the Buddha to the end of his life. Now the path turns to something lighter and very old: the Jataka tales, hundreds of stories that tradition says the Buddha told about his own earlier lives, as an animal, a king, a merchant, a monkey. They were painted on temple walls and carved on stone gates, and they've been told to children for more than two thousand years. The first one this week begins in a forest, with four friends: an otter, a jackal, a monkey, and a hare.
screen: `A RABBIT IN THE MOON.` → `THE JATAKA: EARLIER LIVES.` → `FOUR FRIENDS IN A FOREST.`

segments.voice: The hare is wise, and he teaches the others. One day he says: tomorrow is a holy day. Let's keep it well, and if anyone comes asking for food, let's give from what we have. The next morning, each goes out. The otter finds fish on a riverbank. The jackal finds some meat and a pot of curds. The monkey brings mangoes. But the hare only eats grass. And he thinks: I can't offer anyone grass. If a hungry guest comes, I'll give him my own body. Now, the king of the gods, Sakka, hears about this and decides to test it. He comes down disguised as a hungry traveler, and visits each friend in turn. The otter offers fish. The jackal offers meat. The monkey offers mangoes. Then he comes to the hare. And the hare says: gather some wood and make a fire. I'll give you something I've never given before. The fire is lit. The hare shakes himself three times, so that any tiny creatures in his fur can escape and won't be harmed. And he leaps into the flames. But the fire is cold. Not a hair on him is singed. The traveler reveals himself as Sakka. He says he came only to test him. And so that the hare's gift will be remembered for as long as the world lasts, he draws the hare's image on the face of the moon. You don't have to believe the moon has a hare on it to feel what the story is doing. The hare had the least of anyone. And he gave the most, the one thing he had. Even then, he shook himself first, so he wouldn't hurt the fleas.
screen: `FOUR FRIENDS, ONE HOLY DAY.` · `THE HARE ONLY HAS GRASS.` · `HE SHAKES HIMSELF THREE TIMES.` · `DRAWN ON THE MOON.` · then, large: `GIVE WHAT YOU HAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find what you have to give. Settle and breathe. Maybe it feels like you don't have much today. Not much money, not much energy. Ask yourself, like the hare: what do I actually have? Time. Attention. A skill. A listening ear. A good laugh. Pick one. Picture giving it, fully, to someone who needs it. And tonight, if you can, look up for the hare in the moon. The bell holds the time.
The hare in the moon. A hare with only grass offered his whole self to a hungry guest, and his image was drawn on the moon.
screen: `THE HARE IN THE MOON — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: give what you have. Today, give one thing you actually have, time, attention, a skill, instead of waiting until you have more. Day eighty-five.

86.title: The banyan deer
86.hook: a deer king takes the place of a pregnant doe; the hunting king is moved to stop the hunt (Jataka 12)
86.howItsDone: The banyan deer story is one of the best known Jataka tales, often told in Buddhist schools and temples to illustrate compassion and self-sacrifice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hare in the moon, who had only grass and gave himself. Your line was give what you have. Did you see him last night? Day eighty-six.

Have you ever taken someone's shift so they could be at a birth, or a funeral, or just sleep? Somebody's turn was coming, and you stepped in. Long ago, the story goes, the king of Benares loved to hunt deer, and every day he dragged the townspeople out of their fields to help. The people got tired of it. So they drove a whole forest of deer into the king's park and shut the gate, and said: there. Now hunt them there. In that park were two herds, each with its own king. One was a golden deer called Banyan. That's our hero. The other was called Branch.
screen: `TAKING SOMEONE'S SHIFT.` → `A KING WHO LOVED TO HUNT.` → `TWO HERDS IN ONE PARK.`

segments.voice: Every day the king or his cook came and shot at the deer, and many were wounded in the chaos, not just the one taken. So Banyan went to Branch and proposed a grim deal. Instead of this, let's draw lots. One deer each day goes to the chopping block on its own, and the herds take turns. Fewer will suffer. And the king, who admired the two golden deer, had already promised that he would never kill their leaders. One day the lot falls on a doe in Branch's herd who is about to give birth. She goes to her king and asks: let me have my fawn first, and then I'll go. Branch refuses. It's your turn. Go. So she goes to the other king, Banyan, and asks him. And Banyan says: go home. I'll take your turn. He walks to the block, and lays his head down on it. The cook runs to tell the king. The king comes, and says: but I spared you. Why are you here? And the deer explains about the doe. And the king is moved beyond words. He says: I have never seen such kindness, even among people. Get up. I spare your life and hers. And Banyan says: and the rest of the deer? Them too. And the other animals in the forest? Them too. And the birds? And the fish in the water? One by one, the deer king asks, until every creature has been given its safety. Tradition says this was one of the Buddha's earlier lives. The Jataka ends with a verse that boils down to this: better to stay close to Banyan than to live with Branch.
screen: `A GRIM DEAL: ONE A DAY.` · `THE DOE'S TURN COMES.` · `I'LL TAKE YOUR TURN.` · `SAFETY FOR EVERY CREATURE.` · then, large: `STAND IN FOR SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one hard turn you could take for someone today. Settle and breathe. Think of the people around you. Who's carrying something heavy right now? A new parent. A worn-out coworker. A friend with a sick relative. Picture one of them. Now picture yourself stepping in for one small thing. The dishes. The school run. A phone call they dread. You don't have to lay your head on a block. Just take one turn. The bell holds the time.
The banyan deer. A golden deer king who took a pregnant doe's turn at the block, and moved a hunting king to spare every creature.
Your line: stand in for someone. Today, take one hard turn off someone else's list without being asked. Day eighty-six.

87.title: The talkative tortoise
87.hook: two geese carry a tortoise on a stick; he opens his mouth to answer the jeers and falls (Jataka 215)
87.howItsDone: The talkative tortoise is a favorite Jataka for children across Buddhist Asia, and Buddhist teaching counts right speech, including knowing when not to speak, as part of the eightfold path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the banyan deer, who laid his head on the block in a mother's place. Your line was stand in for someone. Whose turn did you take? Day eighty-seven.

You've typed the perfect comeback. Your thumb is hovering over send. Someone in the comments said something smug, and you know exactly what to say back. Hold that feeling. Long ago, the story goes, the king of Benares talked too much. Nobody else could get a word in. His wise adviser, who tradition says was the Buddha in an earlier life, had been waiting for a way to tell him so without getting in trouble. And one day, a tortoise fell out of the sky and landed in the palace courtyard, split in two. The king asked how on earth that happened. And the adviser told him.
screen: `THE PERFECT COMEBACK.` → `A KING WHO TALKED TOO MUCH.` → `A TORTOISE FALLS FROM THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Up in the mountains, a tortoise lived in a lake, and two young wild geese used to come there to feed. They became friends. One day the geese said: come home with us. We live in a golden cave in the Himalayas. It's beautiful. And the tortoise said: how? I can't fly. The geese had an idea. We'll hold the two ends of a stick in our beaks. You bite down on the middle. And we'll fly you there. Just one thing. You have to keep your mouth shut the whole way. Not a word. So off they go, a goose at each end, the tortoise clamped on the middle, flying over the countryside. They pass over a village, and the children look up, and start shouting: look, look! Two geese carrying a tortoise on a stick! And the tortoise gets angry. He wants to say: if my friends want to carry me, what's it to you, you brats? He opens his mouth to say it. And he lets go of the stick. And down he falls, right into the king's courtyard. Now the adviser turns to the king and says, gently, this is what happens to people who can't hold their tongue. The Jataka says the king understood the story was about him, and from then on he spoke less. What's so good about this one is that the tortoise isn't wicked. He isn't even wrong. The kids really were being rude. He just couldn't let it go unanswered. And that one reply cost him everything. The same story is told in other Indian fable collections too, like the Panchatantra. It traveled because everyone recognized the tortoise. It's us, with our thumb over send.
screen: `A STICK, TWO GEESE, ONE TORTOISE.` · `KEEP YOUR MOUTH SHUT.` · `HE OPENS HIS MOUTH TO ANSWER.` · `THE KING SPOKE LESS.` · then, large: `NOT EVERY WORD NEEDS SAYING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one retort go unsaid, and practice it now. Settle and breathe. Remember a moment when someone said something that stung, and you wanted to fire back. Feel the words rise, the heat in your jaw. Now, like the tortoise on the stick, keep your mouth closed. Breathe through your nose. Feel the words, and let them stay unspoken. Notice that you're still flying. The bell holds the time.
The talkative tortoise. Carried through the sky on a stick by two geese, he opened his mouth to answer the jeers, and fell.
Your line: not every word needs saying. Today, let one comeback go unsent, and see what happens. Day eighty-seven.

88.title: The quarrelling quails
88.hook: the quails lift the net together and fly off, until they start to bicker (Jataka 33)
88.howItsDone: The quail story is told in Buddhist communities as a lesson in harmony, and harmony in the sangha, the monastic community, is something Buddhist monastic rules work hard to protect.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the talkative tortoise, who opened his mouth to answer the jeers, and fell. Your line was not every word needs saying. Which comeback did you let go? Day eighty-eight.

Any group that's ever pulled off something hard together, a band, a team, a family moving house, knows the moment it starts to go wrong. It's rarely the big challenge that breaks it. It's the small stuff. Who left the dishes. Who didn't pull their weight. Long ago, the story goes, a flock of many thousands of quails lived in a forest, led by a wise quail. Tradition says that was the Buddha, in an earlier life. And a bird-catcher lived nearby. He'd imitate the quail call, and when they gathered, he'd throw his net over them, and carry them off to sell. So the wise quail made a plan.
screen: `IT'S RARELY THE BIG CHALLENGE.` → `THOUSANDS OF QUAILS, ONE LEADER.` → `A BIRD-CATCHER'S NET.`

segments.voice: When the net falls on us, the leader says, every one of you put your head through a hole in the mesh. Then all together, lift, and fly. Carry the net to a thorn bush, drop it there, and slip out from underneath. And it works. The next time the bird-catcher throws his net, thousands of little heads pop up through the mesh, and the whole net rises into the air like a sail and floats off to a thorn bush. The bird-catcher spends the evening untangling his net from the thorns, empty-handed. Day after day. His wife starts asking questions. Then one day, as the quails are landing to feed, one of them accidentally steps on another's head. Who stepped on my head? I did, sorry, I didn't mean it. But the other one won't let it go. And the argument grows. Oh, I suppose you think you're the one lifting the whole net by yourself? The wise quail sees it and knows: when quarreling starts, disaster isn't far behind. And he leads the quails who'll follow him away to another place. The bird-catcher, meanwhile, bides his time. A few days later he throws his net again, over the ones who stayed. And they're still bickering. You lift it. No, you lift it. I lifted it last time, your turn. And while they argue about who should lift, nobody lifts at all. The bird-catcher gathers the net and carries them all away. It's a story about an enemy, but the enemy isn't what beats them. The net was always there. It only closed when they stopped lifting together.
screen: `HEADS THROUGH THE MESH, AND LIFT.` · `THE NET FLOATS OFF LIKE A SAIL.` · `WHO STEPPED ON MY HEAD?` · `NOBODY LIFTS AT ALL.` · then, large: `TOGETHER WE LIFT THE NET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cooperate on one small thing, starting with how you think about it. Settle and breathe. Think of a group you belong to, a family, a team, a household. Is there a small squabble going on? Who does what. Whose turn it is. Picture everyone under the same net. Now picture yourself, instead of arguing about who should lift, just lifting. Your end. No score kept. The bell holds the time.
The quarrelling quails. Together they lifted the bird-catcher's net and flew free, until they started bickering about who was lifting.
Your line: together we lift the net. Today, pick up one shared job without asking whose turn it is. Day eighty-eight.

91.title: The ruru deer
91.hook: a golden deer saves a drowning man, who later betrays him to the king
91.howItsDone: Buddhists tell Jataka stories like this one in temples, schools and at home, and many hold up doing good without expecting a return as part of the perfection of giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the golden goose: one feather at a time, until greed pulled them all and the gold turned plain. Your line was greed plucks the goose bare. Did you take only what you needed? Day ninety-one, the last of the short stories.
screen: `THE GOLDEN GOOSE — GREED PLUCKS THE GOOSE BARE.`

segments.voice: You've probably done it. Covered a shift for someone who never covered yours. Lent money and watched it quietly vanish. Held the door, and the person walked through looking at their phone. There's a small voice that says: next time, don't bother. Today's story is for that voice. It's number 482 in the Jataka, the collection of tales about the Buddha's earlier lives. A deer with a coat like gold, a river in flood, and a man shouting for help. It's a short story about a long question: why do good for people who won't thank you?
screen: `YOU COVERED THEIR SHIFT.` → `NEXT TIME, DON'T BOTHER?` → `A RIVER IN FLOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the story. A young man from a rich family has wasted everything he had. Buried in debt, he throws himself into the Ganges. Then, in the water, he changes his mind and screams for help. On the bank lives a ruru deer, the Bodhisatta, the Buddha-to-be, with golden skin and a gentle voice. He wades into the current, lets the man grab hold, and carries him to shore. He warms him, feeds him, shows him the road home. He asks one thing: don't tell anyone where I live. The man promises. Meanwhile, in the city, the queen dreams of a golden deer teaching the law, and she asks the king to find him. The king offers a reward: a village, and a thousand coins. And the man he saved hears it and goes straight to the palace. He leads the king to the river. The king raises his bow. The deer speaks, in a human voice, and asks who showed him the way. When the king hears the whole story, he's so disgusted he wants to shoot the traitor instead. And here's the turn that makes it a Jataka. The deer steps between them and asks the king to spare the man. He's still saving him. The king lets him go, takes the deer to the city with honor, and the deer teaches the court. So what's the point? Not that people are awful. The story is honest that some are. The point is where the deer's goodness lives. It never depended on the man's gratitude. It came from the deer. The ingratitude doesn't cancel the rescue. It just shows who each of them was.
screen: `A MAN IN THE FLOOD.` · `THE DEER CARRIES HIM OUT.` · `THE MAN SELLS HIM TO THE KING.` · `THE DEER SAVES HIM AGAIN.` · then, large: `DO IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one good thing you did that nobody thanked you for. Feel whatever comes: the sting, the little scorekeeping. Don't push it away. Now picture the deer on the riverbank, choosing to wade in. Let the act you did stand on its own, finished and complete, whether or not anyone saw. Breathe with that. If a thought comes up about what they owe you, let it float past like a leaf on the river. The bell holds the time.
The ruru deer. The golden deer who saved a drowning man, was betrayed by him, and then saved him again.
Your line: do it anyway. Today, do one kind thing for someone who probably won't notice, and don't mention it. Day ninety-one.
